title: The Long Read: What a River Remembers
intro: A slow argument about sediment, memory and the stories a catchment keeps long after the flood has gone.

add_image.image_alt: A river running through a wooded valley
add_image.image_caption: The upper catchment, three days after the flood peak.

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph: Rivers are often described as corridors, which is a way of saying they carry things from one place to another. Sediment, nutrients, plastic, heat. The metaphor is useful and slightly wrong: a river also keeps things. It slows them, sorts them, and lets them settle into layers that outlast the event that moved them.

That capacity to hold is what makes a catchment readable. A core taken from a floodplain is not a record of one flood but of many, each written in a different grain size, each interrupted by the next. The archive is not tidy. It is, however, honest.

add_quote.text: A flood is an event. A floodplain is a memory of events, edited by every one that follows.

add_content_to_page.add_paragraph: We spend a lot of time measuring what leaves a catchment — the export of carbon, the pulse of nitrate after rain. Less time is spent on what stays. Yet the staying is what makes the landscape legible: the shape of a bank, the depth of a soil, the age of a seed bank waiting under a pasture.

The practical consequence is unglamorous. If you want to know what a river will do next, the most useful instrument may not be a gauge but a spade. The past is not a prediction, but it is a constraint, and constraints are what models are made of.

add_special_note.heading: A note on method
add_special_note.text: This essay draws on four years of floodplain cores and a reading of the catchment's land-use record. Neither is a substitute for the other.
